overview: Two standard ways to test whether an antibiotic will actually work against a specific isolate — one qualitative, one quantitative.
genZNote: A ring on a plate versus an actual number.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: A qualitative method (Kirby-Bauer) where antibiotic-impregnated disks are placed on an inoculated agar plate and zones of inhibition are measured.
aspects.valueB: A quantitative method where an organism is exposed to serial two-fold dilutions of an antibiotic in broth to determine the lowest concentration that inhibits visible growth (MIC).

aspects.label: Type of Result Produced
aspects.valueA: Categorical: susceptible, intermediate, or resistant, based on zone diameter.
aspects.valueB: Numeric: an exact minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) in µg/mL.

aspects.label: Quantitative Precision
aspects.valueA: Does not give an exact concentration, only a category.
aspects.valueB: Gives a precise concentration value, useful for dosing decisions in critical infections.

aspects.label: Automation Potential
aspects.valueA: Largely manual, though zone reading can be automated with imaging systems.
aspects.valueB: Well suited to automated systems (e.g. broth microdilution panels, automated readers).

aspects.label: Turnaround Time and Cost
aspects.valueA: Relatively simple and inexpensive, standard 16–24 hour incubation.
aspects.valueB: Similar turnaround time but generally requires more standardized equipment/panels, and can cost more per test.

aspects.label: When MIC Value Specifically Matters
aspects.valueA: Not applicable — Kirby-Bauer doesn't provide the numeric MIC needed for this.
aspects.valueB: Preferred for serious infections (e.g. endocarditis, bacteremia) or when dosing needs to be tailored to a precise MIC/PK-PD target.
